newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: U.N. Zaire envoy heads for S.Africa to plan summit.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Zaire envoy heads for S.Africa to plan summit.

text.p: U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun will return to South Africa on Thursday to settle a date and a venue for direct talks between the battling parties in Zaire, South African Deputy Foreign Minister Aziz Pahad said.
Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila had both reaffirmed their commitment to a negotiated peace, he said, adding:
"The only issue now outstanding is that we need to determine the time and the place where the meeting should take place."
South African President Nelson Mandela last week formally invited Mobutu to South Africa to meet Kabila face-to-face for the first time.
Mobutu's envoy, Honore Ngbanda, flew into South Africa on Wednesday and met Deputy President Thabo Mbeki and other officials to convey Mobutu's official response.
"(Ngbanda) conveyed the message that the Zairean government remains committed to having the meeting," Pahad said, leaving only the issue of a date and venue.
Pahad said representatives of both sides agreed during talks earlier this month in Pretoria that negotiations were necessary to end the war.

"Both parties agreed that negotiations must lead to fundamental and democratic change and therefore there was a need for a process of transition leading to transparent, fair and inclusive elections, which would be organised and supervised by an independent body and would be monitored by the international community.
"The ultimate objective of any negotiation must be to achieve a genuine democracy in Zaire," he said.
Pahad did not reveal details of Mobutu's response, but he indicated that the ailing Zairean president, who has ruled his country for 32 years, had rejected a South African venue.
Mobutu favours talks in neighbouring Congo, a country that has been sympathetic to his government, while Kabila wanted to meet in Lubumbashi, Zaire's second city, which is under rebel control.
South African government sources said Mandela had told both sides their proposals were unacceptable, but had said he was not committed to a meeting in his own country.
Pahad said Sahnoun, who also represents the Organisation of African Unity in his efforts to end the war, had visited Angola and Namibia and was returning to South Africa on Thursday evening.
"We will have consultations with him and other interested role players to finally determine the time and the venue of this very important summit," he said.
Pahad said a settlement in Zaire, where rebels have seized control of over half of the land, including the economic backbone, was crucial to the stability of the entire continent.
"It is clear to us that if instability continues in Zaire, it will affect not only the nine bordering countries, but even countries such as South Africa.
"We seriously believe that the very new democracy that has been established in Angola could be threatened by developments in Zaire," he said.
"We in South Africa as well as the United Nations and the OAU believe that a negotiated solution in Zaire is in the interests of the Zairean people as a whole."
